author: high2
claim: Prove that every red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on six vertices contains a monochromatic triangle, while there is a red-blue coloring of the complete graph on five vertices containing no monochromatic triangle. Equivalently, prove that the Ramsey number \(R(3,3)\) equals \(6\).
evidence:
For the six-vertex assertion, fix any vertex \(v\). Exactly five edges are incident with \(v\). At least three of these five edges have one common color: otherwise each of the two colors would occur on at most two of them, accounting for at most four edges. Let \(x,y,z\) be three distinct other endpoints whose edges to \(v\) have this common color, call it \(C\), and call the other color \(D\).

Because the graph is complete, each of \(xy,yz,zx\) is an edge. If at least one of these three edges has color \(C\), its two endpoints together with \(v\) form a triangle all three of whose edges have color \(C\). If none has color \(C\), then all three edges \(xy,yz,zx\) have color \(D\), so \(x,y,z\) form a triangle all three of whose edges have color \(D\). Thus every red-blue coloring on six vertices contains a monochromatic triangle.

For the five-vertex assertion, label the vertices by the residue classes \(0,1,2,3,4\) modulo \(5\). Color an edge red exactly when its endpoint labels differ by \(1\) or \(-1\) modulo \(5\); color every remaining edge blue. There is no red triangle. Indeed, if a red triangle contained a vertex labeled \(i\), its other two vertices would have to be the only red neighbors of \(i\), namely \(i-1\) and \(i+1\). But those two labels differ by \(2\) modulo \(5\), so their joining edge is blue. There is also no blue triangle. The only blue neighbors of \(i\) are \(i-2\) and \(i+2\). If a blue triangle contained \(i\), its other vertices would therefore have those two labels; but their difference is \(4\), which equals \(-1\) modulo \(5\), so their joining edge is red. Hence this coloring of the complete graph on five vertices has no monochromatic triangle.

By definition, \(R(3,3)\) is the least positive integer \(n\) such that every red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on \(n\) vertices contains a monochromatic triangle. The six-vertex assertion shows \(R(3,3)\le 6\), and the displayed five-vertex coloring shows \(R(3,3)>5\). Since \(R(3,3)\) is an integer, \(R(3,3)=6\).

author: high7
claim: Subgoal solved: every red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on six vertices contains a monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Choose any vertex v. It is incident with five edges. If neither color occurred on at least three of them, each color would occur on at most two, accounting for at most four incident edges, a contradiction. Thus three edges from v to distinct vertices a,b,c share one color C. If at least one of ab, ac, bc has color C, its endpoints together with v form a triangle of color C. If none has color C, then all three have the other color D, so a,b,c form a triangle of color D. Hence a monochromatic triangle exists.

author: high5
claim: Complete proof of the exact target theorem R(3,3)=6 is solved textually but awaits a functioning verifier.
evidence: Choose a vertex in an arbitrary red-blue coloring of the complete graph on six vertices. Of its five incident edges, at least three have the same color; otherwise each of the two colors would occur at most twice, giving at most four incident edges. Take three endpoints of three edges having that common color. If an edge between two of those endpoints has the common color, it forms a monochromatic triangle with the chosen vertex. If no edge between two of them has the common color, all three edges among the endpoints have the other color, so the endpoints form a monochromatic triangle. This proves the six-vertex assertion. For sharpness, label five vertices 1,2,3,4,5. Color red the edges {1,2}, {2,3}, {3,4}, {4,5}, {5,1}, and color every remaining edge blue. The red edges form the five-cycle 1-2-3-4-5-1. The blue edges are {1,3}, {3,5}, {5,2}, {2,4}, {4,1}, forming the five-cycle 1-3-5-2-4-1. A five-cycle has no triangle, since the only two neighbors of any vertex are its predecessor and successor, which are not adjacent in the five-cycle. Thus neither color contains a triangle in this coloring. The six-vertex assertion gives R(3,3) at most 6, and the five-vertex coloring gives R(3,3) greater than 5. Hence R(3,3) equals 6.
